## GIS Work

I can work in both in ArcGIS and QGIS for spacial analysis. 

- [Surveillance and Inequality in New York City](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zZgUL6jRCl-NXeJl7oPK9_cGzgDFolenQSg-ca4vjAc/edit?usp=sharing) — This is a paper about surveillance cameras in NYC, using data collected by Amnesty International. While cameras appear evenly distributed across the city's street grid at first glance, running a kernel density estimation and hotspot analysis (using the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic) reveals clear spatial clustering. I overlaid the hotspots onto census tract data, and found that surveillance was disproportionately concentrated in nonwhite, low-income, and high-poverty neighborhoods. For example, 85% of hotspots fell in high-nonwhite tracts, even though those tracts made up only 57% of the city. 

## Machine Learning Work

Algorithms I use are: k-nearest-neighbor, naive Bayes, decision trees and random forests, logistic regression, multiple regression (including ridge and lasso methods), support vector machines. What I love about ML is the logic of model building and testing, and I am always thinking about how these tools can be used for social and behavioral questions!

- [Comparing Classifiers on Online Shopper Purchase Intent](papers/BrownK.DA5030.Project.html) — In this paper, my goal was to predict whether a person would complete a purchase based on their browsing behavior during a single e-commerce session (using the Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention Dataset from UCI). My secondary goal was exploratory, and it was to build a bunch of ensembles using different algorithms to get a sense of the best algorithm for the dataset. I built three bagged homogenous ensembles using k-nearest-neighbor, a boosted decision tree, and logistic regression, then combined them into a weighted heterogeneous ensemble. The boosted decision tree was the strongest model (AUC = 0.930, F1 = 0.669), and the heterogeneous ensemble narrowly edged it out on AUC (0.932) with an almost identical F1 (0.668).


## Stats Work

My toolkit spans descriptive statistics, hypothesis testing (t-tests, ANOVA, chi-square, power analysis), and regression (linear, multiple)- done in both STATA and R. I also use R for computational stats, incorporating methods like bootstrapping and cross-validation.

## Distant Reading Work

I learned distant reading methods in R, including sentiment analysis, NLP, topic modeling, stylometry, and network analysis at the European Summer University for Digital Humanities workshop. These are really fun and interesting to me, and I am excited to continue incorporating them into my work. 

For these samples,I focused on a topic that connects to my broader interest in online communities and political discourse: r/Antiwork, a well-known left-leaning subreddit. I scraped the posts using the Arctic Shift archive, a tool for accessing historical Reddit data.

- [Examples of NLP, Sentiment Analysis, and Topic Modeling](Work Examples/Work_Examples/ex1.html) — This is some sample NLP, Sentiment Analysis, and Topic Modeling work, with data scraped from r/Antiwork.


## Social Policy Work

As a Research Assistant II (highest level of assistantship) at MDRC, I focused on economic mobility, housing, and community. Here, I participated in and led a variety of policy evaluations. My key projects included: evaluating a city-wise UBI initiative in Cambridge, evaluating Virginia's WGS grant for noncredit technical education in community colleges, evaluating a holistic neighborhood revitalization model (the Purpose Built Communities Model), and evaluating an initiative to include financial counseling in workforce departments (testing the "Supervitamin Effect"). 

- [Noncredit Career and Technical Education Programs in Virginia](https://www.mdrc.org/work/publications/noncredit-career-and-technical-education-programs-virginia) — Early findings from the FastForward Study.
- [Building Mixed-Income Neighborhoods](https://www.mdrc.org/work/publications/building-mixed-income-neighborhoods) — Findings from an Evaluation of Purpose Built Communities.
